newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Canadian markets seen boosted by budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Canadian markets seen boosted by budget.

text.p: Canadian financial markets were expected to benefit from the federal budget due out on Tuesday, although analysts said that much of the good news was already priced in.

"There are expectations built in that it will be a very good budget, so it's hard to surpass those expectations. Nevertheless, I think that you might see some follow-through, positive reaction one or two days later," said Mark Chandler, senior economist with Goldman Sachs Canada.

Finance Minister Paul Martin's budget for the 1997-1998 fiscal year was widely expected to be a market-friendly document that further reduced the deficit and relied on conservative interest rate and economic growth assumptions.

Martin was not expected to change his deficit targets of C$17 billion for the 1997-98 fiscal year and C$9 billion for fiscal 1998-99. But investors expected Martin to base his budget on such conservative assumptions that actual deficits turned out much lower.

"If we come around to the view that the underlying deficit is closer to C$10 billion for this year and closer to zero for fiscal 1998-1999, I think the markets are going to look at this as a good news budget, but it may take some time to build," said David Rosenberg, senior economist with Nesbitt Burns.

The biggest concern of financial markets was that Martin would hike spending with his government expected to call an election this year. Martin has said he intended to include some new spending to battle child poverty.
If new spending totaled only about C$1 billion, analysts said the budget would be well received by financial markets in the days after the release.

"It's going to be a positive budget but no real surprises. In that sense I'm wondering how much you can really get out of the budget. But I think there's scope for a type of relief rally in Canadian bonds and the currency," said Harvinder Kalirai, Canadian analyst with New York-based financial analysis firm I.D.E.A.
Analysts said that financial markets had strengthened due to budget optimism. Canadian bonds benefited the most, as seen in their performance against U.S. treasuries.

The spread between Canadian and U.S. 30-year bond yields narrowed to 24 basis points at the close of trading on Thursday, the lowest since early November. Canadian 10-year bonds on Thursday also put in their best performance against comparable U.S. treasuries this year.

The Canadian dollar also strengthened on Thursday and Friday, closing above the key C$1.3514 (US$0.74) level on Thursday. Traders attributed some of the gains to optimism about the budget. The impact of budget optimism on equities was harder to discern, analysts said.
Goldman's Chandler said that with the recent gains in bonds, the positive impact of the budget on Tuesday would likely have the largest effect on the currency.
Analysts said that if more good news was priced into financial markets ahead of the budget, there was an increased risk that markets would trade flat or even weaken immediately after the budget.

"The actual budget itself I don't think is going to lead to much of a reaction," said Dan Kelly, director of financial markets research with CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Inc. "There's a potential for a slight negative surprise with these election goodies. That to me is the kind of market reaction that could occur."
